The bull case is that TUI is a genuinely good business wearing a bad balance sheet, and the market is still pricing the balance sheet it had in 2021 rather than the one it has now.

Start with what is not in dispute. TUI has grown profits four years running: a EUR 2.48bn loss in 2021, a EUR 213m loss in 2022, then EUR 306m, EUR 507m and EUR 636m of net income through 2025. Revenue reached EUR 24.18bn last year. Trailing-twelve-month earnings per share are EUR 1.26, so at EUR 7.10 the shares change hands for about 5.6 times what the company actually earns today. That is not a forecast; it is the tape.

The engine underneath is the part the market keeps ignoring. Over 80% of profit comes from what TUI calls Holiday Experiences — 463 owned or managed hotels, 18 cruise ships, and the Musement experiences marketplace. Those assets ran at 84% occupancy across the full year and 88% in the fourth quarter (December 2025 call), which management noted is "significantly higher than what you see with others", with daily rates up 3% to 5% in a soft market. Cruise returns were stated at 22% and 17%. Occupancy on the ships is at or above 100% — the chief executive volunteered that last summer hit 108%, "so maybe we even had too many kids on board". The reason these assets stay full is the second half of the model: TUI owns its own shops, apps and airlines, so it fills its own beds without paying an online travel agency a toll. A 35-million-customer database does the marketing that a rival has to buy.

The balance sheet is the part that has actually changed, and it is verifiable rather than narrated. Between December 2025 and March 2026 total debt fell from EUR 6.91bn to EUR 4.47bn. Net debt is down about EUR 0.5bn year on year. The 2028 convertible bond was repaid early. The final Marella cruise ship was bought out of its lease into ownership. Interest expense is improving by roughly EUR 10m a year as a direct consequence. And in February 2026 the company paid its first dividend in years — the single hardest signal a board can send about the durability of its cash, because unlike a forecast it costs real money.

The transformation has also started to show first evidence rather than first slides. Markets & Airline — five or six separate national airlines being welded into one, with one booking system, one buying system and a single web platform — improved by EUR 10m year on year in the first quarter of 2026 even while absorbing a EUR 6m hit from the Jamaica hurricane. Belgium and the Netherlands, the chronic problem markets, turned first after the airline was given commercial control, which is precisely the test the model had to pass. Denied-boarding compensation is running at a third of its former level simply because a Belgian aircraft can now cover a German grounding.

There are three free options the market is not paying for. First, cruise pricing: the business is sold out and cannot raise price this year because the inventory is already booked, but management has conceded it could have charged 3% to 4% more — that is a 2027 and 2028 repricing, not a lost opportunity. Second, the tours and city-trips adjacency, where TUI holds 3% and 5% share of markets it believes should be 30% — an unpenetrated field it is entering with a preproduced round-trip product. Third, Musement is now wholesaling its platform to Booking.com, easyJet, lastminute.com and, since February 2026, Jet2 — capital-free fee income sold to TUI's own competitors, buried in a bullet point.

For this to work, three conditions must hold. The Middle East must normalise so that Eastern Mediterranean and long-haul demand returns — management assumes this takes until the end of the calendar year. Kerosene must stay where it is; Brent at roughly USD 71 is a live tailwind against the fuel costs that caused the April downgrade in the first place. And the cost programme must convert on schedule, with the single web platform reaching Germany in January or February 2027.

If all three hold, this is a company earning EUR 1.5bn or more before interest and tax on a EUR 3.6bn market value, still deleveraging, still paying a dividend, and priced at roughly five times earnings.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require TUI to be a bad company. It requires only that the shareholder's claim on a good company is thinner than it looks — and that the balance sheet does not permit a second bad year.

Start with the number that indicts everything else. Management quotes cruise returns of 22% and 17%. The group's return on invested capital is 0.4%. Both are true, and the gap between them is the entire bear case. The excellence exists at the property; it does not arrive at the group. What stands in between is EUR 3.02bn of net debt (including EUR 2.32bn of capitalised leases), EUR 1.03bn of minority interests in businesses like the Riu hotel joint venture, and an airline still halfway through being rebuilt. Every euro of hotel margin passes through all of that before it reaches this share. That is why the discount exists, and it is largely correct.

The cheapness is measured against numbers that are going the wrong way. The stock screens at 3.7 times free cash flow — but free cash flow fell 17.4% year on year and is compounding at negative 14.1% over three years, from roughly EUR 991m in 2025 to EUR 722m trailing. Earnings per share are rising while cash generation falls. A low multiple on a shrinking denominator is not a bargain, it is arithmetic. Across four earnings calls, management discussed profit, net debt and interest expense fluently and free cash flow almost not at all; when a UBS analyst pushed twice on capital-expenditure flexibility in May 2026, the answer was "we will have that discussion internally".

The headline quality metric is fake. Return on equity of 99% looks like a franchise. It is an artifact of a bombed-out equity base: EUR 7.98bn of paid-in capital sitting against EUR 6.47bn of accumulated other comprehensive losses, leaving EUR 2.02bn of book equity. A 99% return on equity next to a 0.4% return on capital is not a moat; it is a broken denominator. Any mechanical screen ranking this name on returns is being fooled.

The guidance record broke, and recently. On 10 February 2026 TUI reaffirmed 7% to 10% profit growth for the year. On 22 April 2026 — ten weeks later — it cut to a range of EUR 1.1bn to EUR 1.4bn and suspended revenue guidance entirely. Against the 2025 base of about EUR 1.41bn, that range spans a 22% decline to roughly flat. The four-year growth streak, the thing the bull case rests on, is being broken this year. A EUR 300m range with four and a half months of the year remaining is not guidance; it is an admission that the company cannot forecast its own book. The chief executive conceded exactly that: "the visibility is not as much as we are used to it".

And the damage is worse than the headline. Summer 2026 booked revenue in Markets & Airline was down 7% year on year at the April cut, having been down only 2% in August 2025 — the deterioration accelerated. Hotel occupancy for the second half was tracking 7% below the prior year, concentrated in Turkey, Cyprus and Egypt. This is a late-booking business, so the season cannot be pre-sold out of trouble; management flagged that customers "book very late" and that May was merely flat against last year.

The solvency position leaves no room for a second shock. The Altman-Z score of 1.4 sits in the distress zone. Net debt of EUR 3.02bn exceeds a market capitalisation of EUR 3.6bn — the lenders own more of this enterprise than the shareholders do. Deferred revenue of EUR 5.25bn is customer money for holidays not yet taken; in a demand shock that is a refund liability, not a cushion. And there is no rescue coming from rates: the Federal Reserve is on a hawkish hold with markets pricing roughly a 77% chance of a hike by December, which means a levered European cyclical refinances into a worse market, not a better one.

Management has disclosed a structural cost disadvantage it cannot fix quickly. In May 2026: "we have a significant disadvantage in our fleet. We have now 60 in the summer out of 100, 737 MAX… we don't have the MAX 10 yet. So we don't have a cost competitive product to the A321neo", with "another year to go". A tour operator whose aircraft cost more to fly than a rival's, in a business with a 9.2% gross margin, is losing a race it has not finished entering. Separately, Ebel refused to match UK rivals loosening payment terms — principled, and a share-loss risk he did not price.

The pricing power the bulls cite is not showing up where it counts. Occupancy rose. Daily rates rose 3% to 5%. Gross margin was 9.2% and described as stable. The margin did not move. Whatever the hotels are earning is being consumed before it reaches the group line.

Finally, nobody inside is buying. The insider buy ratio is zero across a year in which the chief executive said "investment in TUI is a great thing". The smart-money score is 12 out of 100.

What would confirm the bear: a third-quarter print in August 2026 landing at the bottom of the EUR 1.1bn to EUR 1.4bn range; the mid-August ceasefire expiry re-escalating and taking kerosene with it; or free cash flow turning negative and stalling the deleveraging that is the only thing genuinely working.
consensus_delta:
For a deep-value name the question is not whether the market is excited — it is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company whose earning power is actually stable or growing. Here the honest answer is: partly, and less than it first appears.

**Where the market is genuinely wrong.** The street is still underwriting TUI as the 2021 balance sheet — a company that lost EUR 2.48bn and diluted its owners to survive. That company no longer exists. Total debt fell from EUR 6.91bn to EUR 4.47bn in the single quarter to March 2026. The 2028 convertible bond was repaid *early* — a levered borrower with a liquidity problem does not retire debt ahead of schedule. The final Marella ship was bought out of its lease into ownership. A dividend was paid in February 2026. Four consecutive years of profit growth were delivered, not promised. That is a company actively repairing itself, and it trades at 5.6 times what it earns.

**Where the market is right and this committee will not pretend otherwise.** The peer check kills the easy version of the trade. Jet2, the closest listed comparable, trades at 7.18 times earnings today with *net cash*. TUI trades at 5.6 times with EUR 3.02bn of net debt. The discount is roughly 21% and it is exactly what leverage should cost. There is no 80% mispricing here — the screener's +81% discounted-cash-flow margin of safety is an artifact of extrapolating cash flow that is in fact *falling* 17.4% a year. The whole European package-holiday lane has de-rated together on the same drivers. Cheap versus its own history is not the same as cheap versus the world.

**The specific street assumption that is wrong.** Published targets cluster around EUR 10.2 to 10.4, with Morgan Stanley at EUR 10.50 (trimmed from EUR 11.50) and Jefferies stepping back to neutral after the recent rally. Those numbers embed a recovery to the guided growth path. But nobody appears to have re-anchored to what the peer group actually trades at *now*: at Jet2's live 7.18 times, TUI's trailing earnings support EUR 9.05, and a sum-of-the-parts built from management's own 80/15 profit split, charged properly for EUR 3.02bn of net debt and EUR 1.03bn of minority interests, independently gives EUR 9.06. Two methods, one cent apart. The street is roughly 12% too high, not too low — the market is closer to right than the analysts are.

**The real disagreement, and it is narrow.** The market is treating a 0.4% return on invested capital as the company's earning power. It is not — it is the *shareholder's claim* on a business whose hotels and ships earn 17% to 22%. The distinction matters, and the market conflates the two. But the conflation is only about two-thirds wrong. A director owning this share genuinely does receive the leftovers after EUR 3.02bn of debt, EUR 1.03bn of minorities and an unfinished airline take their cut. The gap between EUR 7.10 and EUR 9.10 is what the market is missing. It is real, it is about 28%, and it is not the multi-bagger the screener advertises.
forcing_function:
**The near-dated event: third-quarter results, on or about 12 August 2026** (roughly 27 days from the scan date). This is the only dated event on the board and it is genuinely forcing — not because it is contractual, but because it is arithmetically cornered. The company must narrow a EUR 1.1bn to EUR 1.4bn range with only weeks of its financial year remaining, and the third quarter *is* the summer that decides the number. There is nowhere left to hide a EUR 300m spread. Either the range collapses upward, in which case four years of delivery becomes five and the peer discount is exposed as too wide, or it collapses downward and the dividend restored six months ago comes into question.

**Why this is a soft, non-binding catalyst rather than a hard one — and the distinction is doing real work.** The date is real; the *payout* is not fixed by anything. This is a scheduled earnings report whose outcome is decided by a third party — the Middle East — and by kerosene. Nothing contractual pays the shareholder on that date. It is a single macro binary wearing a calendar, and this committee will not dress it up as an asymmetric special situation. Note also that the ceasefire clock expires around the same mid-August window: the resolution driver and the reporting date are the same factor arriving twice, which concentrates risk rather than diversifying it.

**The catalyst that has already fired, and must not be counted twice.** The dividend initiation — announced December 2025, paid at the February 2026 annual meeting — was the genuine re-rating event for this story. It is spent. Any thesis still leaning on "TUI will restore the dividend" is underwriting a fact from six months ago.

**The slower, more structural forcing functions, in the order they arrive:**
1. **December 2026 — full-year results plus the cost-programme detail.** Management has twice deferred the quantified savings to a December unveiling. The single web platform reaches Germany, the last market, in "January, February '27". December is where 2027 gets guided and where the transformation either prices or does not.
2. **The deleveraging arithmetic itself, continuously.** This is the most reliable engine on the page and it needs no announcement. Net debt down about EUR 0.5bn year on year, the 2028 convertible retired early, ships bought out of leases. With EUR 3.02bn of net debt against a EUR 3.6bn market value, every euro that moves from the lenders' column to the owners' column is worth roughly a euro of equity — mechanically, without any re-rating at all. In a market regime that rewards balance-sheet repair over rate relief, this is the part of the thesis that does not depend on anyone's opinion.
3. **2027–28 cruise pricing.** Sold-out ships that management concedes were underpriced by 3% to 4% reprice as inventory rolls. Real, but two years out and not a catalyst anyone trades.

**What is absent, and should be named.** There is no activist, no strategic review, no announced asset sale, no governance reset, no tender, no sum-of-the-parts breakup process. On the Loeb catalyst-density test this scores poorly: one dated macro-dependent print, one spent dividend, and a slow deleveraging grind. The regime read favours structural special situations in thin lanes — and a levered cyclical waiting on the weather is not one.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are, quite precisely, the risk. This is not a name where you wait through a quiet stretch for a catalyst — the risky window and the catalyst are the same event.

**The season is the whole year, and it is unhedged.** TUI guided its 2026 profit to be "more back-ended very naturally… towards the Summer" (December 2025). That means essentially all of the year's profit is earned between June and September 2026 — the months directly ahead. There is no second attempt. A tour operator cannot re-run a summer.

**And this is a late-booking market, so it cannot be pre-sold out of trouble.** Management flagged that customers now "book very late" and that May was merely level with last year (May 2026). At the April downgrade, Markets & Airline booked revenue for Summer 2026 was 7% below the prior year — having been down only 2% in August 2025. The deterioration is accelerating, and the inventory is risk capacity that must be filled or flown empty.

**The mid-August collision.** Three things land on top of each other. The United States–Iran 60-day ceasefire clock expires around **mid-August 2026** — and it is more fragile than the headline suggests, with a US airstrike on 26 June following an alleged violation and Geneva talks postponed. TUI's **third-quarter results land at roughly the same moment** (about 27 days out from the scan, so approximately 12 August), and that print must narrow a EUR 1.1bn-to-EUR 1.4bn range with only weeks of the year left. Both bear on the same driver. If the ceasefire fails, kerosene rises, the Eastern Mediterranean and long-haul bookings that management already describes as "almost 0" stay at zero, and the print goes to the bottom of the range — all at once, in the same fortnight.

**The cash-flow hump nobody is discussing.** Free cash flow is already falling 17.4% year on year, from roughly EUR 991m to EUR 722m trailing, and management barely mentions it across four calls. Capital expenditure is committed and hard to stop: hotel projects "online and they will be kind of executed", the Boeing delivery portfolio with attached engine and maintenance spend, and two new Marella ships under a signed shipyard contract. When a UBS analyst asked directly in May 2026 how much of that could be cut, the answer was "we will have that discussion internally". That is a company with fixed outflows and a variable summer.

**Deferred revenue is a liability, not a cushion.** There is EUR 5.25bn of customer money on the balance sheet for holidays not yet taken. In a normal season that is free financing. In a demand shock — a re-escalation that makes people cancel rather than book — it converts into a refund obligation at exactly the moment the cash is needed. This is the mechanism that nearly killed the company in 2020, and it is unchanged.

**No rescue from rates.** The Federal Reserve under Chair Warsh is on a hawkish hold with futures pricing roughly a 77% chance of a *hike* by December, and Goldman no longer expects a 2026 cut. A levered European cyclical with EUR 3.02bn of net debt and an Altman-Z of 1.4 refinances into a worse market, not a better one. Any version of this thesis that quietly relies on cheaper money is dead on arrival.

**The one genuine offset.** Brent at roughly USD 71 and West Texas at USD 68.6 are *below* the level that caused the April downgrade — the cut explicitly cited airline fuel costs. Oil deflating is a real, live tailwind into the very season in question, and it is the single best reason the August print could surprise upward rather than downward.
positioning_washout:
This is the weakest leg of the bull case, and it needs saying plainly: **the forced-selling has already happened, years ago, and there is no mechanical seller left to create an entry.**

The classic setup — a yield-focused or index shareholder base compelled to dump into a change of policy — does not exist here, and it is worth walking through why each version fails.

**There is no dividend base to wash out.** The usual mechanic runs backwards at TUI: the company *initiated* a dividend in February 2026 after years of none. Income funds are being given a reason to arrive, not to leave. The washout risk is the mirror image — if the summer disappoints and the board suspends the payout it has just restored, the newly-arrived income holders leave as mechanically as they came. That is a risk of buying now, not a reason to.

**The capitulation is historic, not pending.** The shareholder register was already destroyed: a EUR 2.48bn loss in 2021, a state bailout, and the dilution visible in EUR 7.98bn of paid-in capital sitting against EUR 6.47bn of accumulated other comprehensive losses. Whoever was going to be forced out was forced out then. The 2023 delisting from London to a single Frankfurt listing already ran its own index-driven flush. Those trades are spent.

**Current positioning is apathetic, not extreme — and apathy does not create an edge.** The smart-money score is 12 out of 100 and institutional flow is a neutral 50 out of 100. The shares sit 6% below their 200-day average and 30% up a 52-week range of EUR 6.08 to EUR 9.56 — the middle. Nobody is crowded in and nobody is being carried out. There is no pain trade primed in either direction; this is a name the market has simply stopped caring about. That is a reason for the discount to persist, not to close.

**The tell that matters: nobody inside is buying.** The insider buy ratio is **zero**. Across a year in which the chief executive said "I very much believe investment in TUI is a great thing" (December 2025) and "we are very confident with the guidance" (February 2026), not one insider put personal money behind those words — including through the April downgrade and the subsequent slide. Management is talking a book it is not funding. In a name where the entire bull case is that the market misjudges an inflection insiders can see first, the total absence of insider buying is the most damaging single data point in the file.

**Where a real flush could still come from.** Only one credible mechanism exists: a bottom-of-range third-quarter print in August 2026 alongside a ceasefire failure, which would break the recently-restored dividend and force out the income holders who just arrived, while pushing an Altman-Z of 1.4 into territory that triggers risk-model exclusions. **That** would be the capitulation this thesis is waiting for — and it would arrive at a price starting with a five, not a seven. That is the event to wait for, and it is precisely why the answer today is to wait rather than to buy.
moderator_conclusion:
**The call: wait for the wash-out.** The same conclusion this committee reached last time, at essentially the same price — EUR 7.104 today against EUR 7.076 then — and for the same reasons, which is precisely why it should not move. Nothing dated has changed since our prior read that our prior read did not already know: it explicitly named oil, geopolitics and the European consumer as the tail, and that tail is still the whole story. A re-reading of known facts is not a reason to change a verdict.

**What is true about the value.** TUI has done what it said it would do for four straight years: a EUR 2.48bn loss in 2021 became EUR 636m of profit in 2025, revenue reached EUR 24.18bn, and the balance sheet has been repaired in public — total debt down from EUR 6.91bn to EUR 4.47bn in one quarter, the 2028 convertible retired early, ships bought out of their leases, and a dividend restored in February 2026. The owned assets are genuinely excellent: 84% occupancy rising to 88%, daily rates up 3% to 5% in a soft market, cruise ships running at or above 100% full. Management quantifies its own bad news and concedes its own mistakes. This is not a promotional story and it is not a fraud.

**What is equally true about the claim on it.** The hotels and ships earn 17% to 22%. The group earns 0.4% on its invested capital. That gap is EUR 3.02bn of net debt, EUR 1.03bn of other people's stakes, and an unfinished airline — and it all sits between the assets and this share. Free cash flow is falling 17.4% a year while earnings rise, so the celebrated 3.7-times-cash-flow multiple is measured against a shrinking number. The 99% return on equity is an artifact of a EUR 6.47bn hole in the equity base, not a franchise. And on 22 April 2026 the company withdrew the growth it had reaffirmed only ten weeks earlier, cutting to EUR 1.1bn–EUR 1.4bn and suspending revenue guidance altogether.

**The peer check is what settles it.** Refreshed live rather than recalled: Jet2 trades at 7.18 times earnings *today*, with net cash exceeding its own share price. TUI trades at 5.6 times with EUR 3.02bn of net debt. That is a 21% discount, and leverage earns every point of it. The entire European package-holiday lane has de-rated together on shared drivers — this is sector beta, not a discovery about TUI. Anchoring to that live peer gives EUR 9.05 per share; a sum-of-the-parts built from management's own profit split and charged properly for debt and minorities gives EUR 9.06. Two independent routes, one cent apart. Our base case is **EUR 9.10** — a refinement of the EUR 10.00 we carried before, on better data, not a change of thesis. The screener's EUR 38.00 cash-flow fair value is not credible and we decline to use it.

**What the regime says, and it argues against acting.** The current read rewards hard, dated catalysts and structural special situations in thin lanes; it explicitly penalises theses hanging on one shared macro factor and treats rate relief as dead. TUI fails on both counts. Its only dated event is an earnings print whose outcome is decided by the Middle East and by kerosene — and the ceasefire clock expires in the same mid-August window, so the resolution driver and the report date are the same factor arriving twice. That concentrates risk rather than spreading it. Meanwhile the Federal Reserve is priced at roughly a 77% chance of a *hike* by December: a levered cyclical refinances into a worse market. The one honest offset is that Brent near USD 71 is below the level that caused the April cut — a real tailwind into the very season at issue, and the best reason August could surprise upward.

**Why the numbers say wait rather than buy.** Risking about 44% to the adverse case to make about 28% to the base case is the wrong shape. Only the EUR 14.00 favourable case pays properly, and it needs three conditions to hold together. There is no floor underneath — no deal terms, no net cash, no tender; the restored dividend is the first thing a board cuts when a levered season goes wrong. And nobody inside is buying: the insider buy ratio is zero across a year in which the chief executive called investing in TUI "a great thing". In a thesis whose core claim is that the market cannot see an inflection insiders can, that silence is the most damaging fact in the file.

**The specific event to wait for.** A bottom-of-range third-quarter print around 12 August 2026 alongside a ceasefire failure — which would break the six-month-old dividend, force out the income holders who only just arrived, and push an Altman-Z of 1.4 into territory that trips risk-model exclusions. That is the flush, and it arrives at a price starting with a five. At EUR 5, the same sum-of-the-parts is a genuinely asymmetric position; at EUR 7.10 it is a fair price for a levered claim on a good operator.

**On the two scores.** The catalyst-aware conviction is a 2: no hard catalyst, one shared macro driver, a spent dividend, and a season that has to be waited out rather than underwritten. The value-only conviction is a 3 — deliberately higher. Stripped of the catalyst question and the regime tilt, this is a real business at a real discount: a narrow but genuine moat in owning differentiated holiday supply, a stable trend, four years of delivery, verifiable deleveraging, and roughly 28% to a peer-anchored fair value. It is not a 4, because a 0.4% return on capital, an Altman-Z of 1.4, falling cash generation and a self-disclosed fleet cost disadvantage are real fragilities the discount is correctly charging for. And it is not capped at 3 by structural decline — the moat is narrow rather than eroding, and the artificial-intelligence threat to travel distribution attacks the wrong 15% of this company. You can automate a booking page; you cannot automate away a bed in Mallorca that TUI owns. Over 80% of the profit comes from owning the product, and in an agent-mediated world that half gets *more* valuable, not less. The risk that kills this equity is a bad summer against EUR 3.0bn of debt — cyclical and financial, not secular.
sop_breakdown:
Two independent methods converge on essentially the same number, which is the reason to trust it.

**Method one — sum-of-the-parts on 2026 guidance.** Take the midpoint of the company's own April 2026 range, EUR 1.25bn of underlying operating profit, and split it the way management splits it:
- Holiday Experiences EUR 1,125m at 7.25 times enterprise value to operating profit = **EUR 8,156m**
- Markets & Airline EUR 185m at 5.0 times = **EUR 925m**
- Holding and other negative EUR 60m at 6.0 times = **negative EUR 360m**
- Enterprise value = **EUR 8,721m**
- Less net debt **EUR 3,023m** (including EUR 2,323m of capitalised leases)
- Less minority interests **EUR 1,100m**
- Equity = **EUR 4,598m** ÷ 507.4m shares = **EUR 9.06 per share**

**Method two — the live peer multiple, cross-checked.** Jet2, the closest listed comparable, trades today at 7.18 times trailing earnings. Apply that to TUI's trailing earnings per share of EUR 1.26 and you get **EUR 9.05 per share**.

Two different routes — one built up from segments and charged for debt and minorities, one a straight read across from the nearest live peer — land within one cent of each other. Base case: **EUR 9.10**, about 28% above the EUR 7.104 quoted on 16 July 2026.

**Why this is below the EUR 10.00 this committee carried previously, and below the roughly EUR 10.2 to 10.4 street consensus:** the peer anchor was refreshed live rather than recalled. Jet2 at 7.18 times is a company with net *cash* — its cash per share of GBP 15.34 exceeds its own share price. TUI carries EUR 3.02bn of net *debt*. A levered operator does not deserve the multiple of an unlevered one, so if anything EUR 9.10 is generous. It is a refinement of the same thesis on better data, not a change of view.

**What the model deliberately refuses to do:** it does not use the screener's DCF fair value of EUR 38.00 or its +81% margin of safety. That model implies the shares are worth more than five times the price, which no peer, no multiple and no cash-flow record on this page supports — free cash flow is *falling* 17.4% a year. It also does not add back the EUR 2,111m equity-accounted investment line, because the TUI Cruises joint venture profit is already inside the operating profit being multiplied. And it does not credit the 99% return on equity, which is an artifact of a EUR 6.47bn accumulated-loss hole in the equity base rather than evidence of a franchise.
risk_reward: Unattractive on the levels, and that is the finding rather than an aside. Downside to the adverse case at EUR 4.00 is roughly 44% below the EUR 7.104 price. Upside to the EUR 9.10 base case is roughly 28%. You are risking more than you stand to make to reach the central estimate; only the EUR 14.00 favourable case pays you properly, and that case requires the Middle East to normalise, kerosene to stay low, and the cost programme to land on schedule — three conditions that must all hold together. There is no structural floor beneath the shares: no deal terms, no net cash (the company has EUR 3.02bn of net debt), no tender. The restored dividend is not a floor — it is the first line a board cuts when a levered season goes wrong. The asymmetry only becomes favourable at a materially lower entry price, which is the whole reason this stays a wait rather than a buy.
peer_comps_note:
The peer work is where the apparent bargain gets cut down to size, and it is the most useful thing in this file.

The screener says every method agrees this is cheap: 3.7 times free cash flow, a discounted-cash-flow margin of safety of +81%, owner-earnings +75%, earnings-power value +50%. The peers say something quite different — they say the whole lane is cheap, and TUI is barely cheaper than it should be.

Measured live on 16 July 2026: **Jet2 trades at 7.18 times trailing earnings and 5.55 times free cash flow. On the Beach trades at about 2.0 times enterprise value to operating profit before depreciation.** Both are being priced as if European leisure travel earnings barely survive to the terminal year. Against that, TUI at EUR 7.104 on trailing earnings per share of EUR 1.26 trades at **5.6 times** — a discount to Jet2 of roughly 21%, not the 80% the discounted-cash-flow model advertises.

And that 21% discount is earned, not free. Jet2 holds net **cash** — its cash per share of GBP 15.34 is larger than its own share price, which is why its enterprise value is only about GBP 737m against a market value several times that. TUI holds EUR 3.02bn of net **debt** against a EUR 3.6bn market value. On the Beach is asset-light with net cash. TUI is the only levered name in its own peer group. A company carrying that much debt should trade below its net-cash peers, and it does — by about the amount you would expect.

**The conclusion the director needs:** the cheapness here is overwhelmingly **shared-factor sector beta, not single-name edge.** The European package-holiday lane has de-rated together, on the same unresolved drivers — the European consumer, kerosene, and Middle East geopolitics. Buying TUI because it is cheap versus its own history is really an expression of the view that the whole lane is mispriced; it is not a discovery about TUI specifically. Any idiosyncratic edge here is thin, and the position should not be credited with alpha it does not have. This also disciplines the fair value: anchoring TUI's base case to Jet2's live 7.18 times gives EUR 9.05 per share, and that is the number the sum-of-the-parts independently confirms — not the EUR 38.00 the screener's cash-flow model asserts.
interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — TUI AG (TUI1.DE)

**Prepared:** 2026-07-16 · **Price used:** EUR 7.104 (XETRA, live quote 2026-07-16) · **Signal type:** deep value
**Transcripts reviewed:** FY25 Q3 (2025-08-13), FY25 full-year (2025-12-10), FY26 Q1 (2026-02-10), FY26 Q2/H1 (2026-05-13)

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story TUI tells has stayed remarkably consistent across these four calls — which is itself the finding. This is not a management team that rotates its explanation every quarter to fit the result.

The spine of the story is **vertical integration**: TUI owns the holidays it sells (463 hotels, 18 cruise ships, a tours-and-activities marketplace called Musement) and also owns the shops, apps and airlines that fill them. Chief Executive Sebastian Ebel has repeated the same sentence in effectively every call — the distribution arm exists "to make sure that our assets are full." In August 2025 he framed it as the reason for a record quarter: "we are able to have higher rates for our unique and differentiated products." In December 2025 he put a number on it: "more than 80% of the profit come from Holiday Experiences and only 15% from Markets & Airline." By May 2026 the framing was unchanged.

What has genuinely **expanded** over the year:

- **The cost story became a real story.** In August 2025 Ebel was visibly holding it back — "I was told I should not talk about cost program" — and deferred to a December unveiling. By February 2026 he was claiming "the first benefit of our cost reduction program," and by May 2026 the mechanism had a name: one airline instead of five or six, one booking system, one web platform ("OneWeb") rolling out market by market through to Germany in "January, February '27."
- **Artificial intelligence moved from a feature to a frame.** In August 2025 AI was a search box in the app. By May 2026 Ebel called it "the most disruptive part of the sector" and said "we understand AI not as one additional tool, but a way of how we work" — including "bringing our own AI agents into LLMs and social media." That is a management team that has noticed the distribution layer it owns is the layer most exposed to being automated away, and is trying to get in front of it.
- **Capital returns arrived.** December 2025 introduced the first dividend policy after years of nothing, paid at the February 2026 annual meeting.

What has **contracted**, and this is the important half:

- **The growth target itself.** December 2025 set out "7% to 10%" underlying earnings growth for the 2026 financial year, reaffirmed in February 2026. On **22 April 2026** the company cut it to a range of **EUR 1.1bn to EUR 1.4bn** and suspended revenue guidance entirely, blaming the continuing Iran war. Against the 2025 base of roughly EUR 1.41bn, that range spans anywhere from a 22% decline to roughly flat. The growth story, as guided in December, is gone for this year.
- **Volume ambition quietly gave way to margin defence.** August 2025: summer bookings "minus 2%." December 2025: "another 1 or 2 volume with lower margin doesn't help us." May 2026: "we were more risk adverse and reducing risk capacity." The language walked steadily from growth to protection.

**Narrative arc verdict:** the strategic story is stable and has been honestly maintained; the *financial* story attached to it was withdrawn in April 2026 under macro pressure.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Quarter | The actual numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Fourth consecutive year with significant profit growth" | Dec 2025 | Net income: −EUR 2.48bn (2021) → −EUR 213m (2022) → EUR 306m (2023) → EUR 507m (2024) → EUR 636m (2025). Earnings per share 0.75 → 0.98 → 1.14. | **Confirmed.** This is real, unambiguous, and four years long. |
| "Record performance… revenue rises to EUR 24.2 billion" | Dec 2025 | Revenue EUR 24.18bn, +4.4% year on year, three-year compound growth +13.5%. | **Confirmed**, but note the deceleration: the three-year rate is 13.5% because of the pandemic rebound; the current rate is 4.4% and the company has now suspended revenue guidance altogether. |
| "We reaffirm our FY26 guidance of +7-10% Und. EBIT growth" | Feb 2026 | Cut on 22 April 2026 to EUR 1.1–1.4bn, roughly ten weeks later. | **Did not hold.** The single most damaging item in this dossier. See §4. |
| "Outstanding occupancy… 84%… increase in the daily rate" / "fourth quarter hotel occupancy, 88%" | Dec 2025 | Gross margin 9.2% and described as *stable*; net margin 2.6%. | **Partially confirmed, and revealing.** Occupancy and daily rates genuinely rose, yet group gross margin did not. The pricing power is real at the property level and is being absorbed before it reaches the group line — by the airline, by distribution, by the leased fleet. |
| "The return on Cruise is with 22% and 17%, very, very high" | Dec 2025 | Group return on invested capital: **0.4%.** | **The central divergence.** Both can be true — a genuinely excellent cruise business sitting inside a group whose total invested capital earns essentially nothing. Management quotes the segment; the director must underwrite the group. |
| "Return on equity 99%" (screener) | — | Equity of EUR 2.02bn is propped on EUR 7.98bn of paid-in capital against **EUR −6.47bn of accumulated other comprehensive losses.** | **Artifact, not a quality signal.** A 99% return on equity next to a 0.4% return on capital is arithmetic on a bombed-out equity base, not evidence of a franchise. Any screen ranking this name on return on equity is being fooled. |
| "Net debt improved another EUR 0.5 billion year-on-year" | Feb 2026 | Confirmed on the balance sheet: total debt fell from EUR 6.91bn (Dec 2025) to EUR 4.47bn (Mar 2026); net debt EUR 3.02bn including EUR 2.32bn of capitalised leases (EUR 0.69bn excluding leases). Convertible 2028 repaid early; final Marella ship taken into ownership. | **Confirmed.** The deleveraging is real and is the best-evidenced claim management makes. Altman-Z of 1.4 still sits in the distress zone, but the direction is unambiguous. |
| "Strong 9 months… best ever result" (Q3 FY25) | Aug 2025 | Q3 FY25 earnings before interest and tax EUR 321m, the highest third quarter on record; guidance raised to 9–11% growth and subsequently beaten (FY25 landed at EUR 1.46bn at constant currency). | **Confirmed and over-delivered.** |
| Free cash flow implicitly healthy (P/FCF 3.7x screens cheap) | — | Free cash flow **−17.4% year on year**, three-year compound **−14.1%**; trailing-twelve-month free cash flow EUR 722m versus roughly EUR 991m in FY25. | **Diverges from the earnings story.** Earnings per share are rising (1.14 → 1.26 trailing) while free cash flow is falling. The cheapness on a cash-flow multiple is measured against a declining number. |

**The forensic core:** management's operational claims check out almost line by line. What does *not* check out is the implied leap from "our hotels and ships earn 17–22%" to "this equity is worth a growth multiple." Between the excellent owned assets and the shareholder sit EUR 3.02bn of net debt, EUR 1.03bn of minority interests, an airline in the middle of a five-into-one rebuild, and a 0.4% group return on capital. The company is a good operator of assets it does not fully own the economics of.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining — but from a genuinely high base, and honestly.**

- **August 2025 — peak confidence.** "You hear us in a good mood. There are not many good news today around in the world." Guidance raised. Specific, offensive, forward-leaning.
- **December 2025 — confident and expansive.** "It was an excellent year for us." New dividend policy, new growth targets, market entries (Romania, Italy). Still offensive. But one telling defensive note, unprompted, on Germany: "I don't see any positive impact to any business in Germany" — the chief executive volunteering a negative read on his own home market.
- **February 2026 — confident but hedging on visibility.** "The prediction is more difficult than it has been in recent years" (carried from December). Guidance reaffirmed, but the vocabulary of caution is now standing furniture: "cautious," "well-balanced strategy," "right risk capacity."
- **May 2026 — defensive, and openly frustrated.** "Someone took away the cream on the cake." "We are a little bit frustrated about this." "Short-term, the business will be challenging." And the giveaway on visibility, explaining the enormous EUR 300m guidance range: "the visibility is not as much as we are used to it."

The shift from offensive to defensive language is clear and it tracks the macro, not the strategy. Notably, Ebel does **not** dress it up — he names the cost of Jamaica (EUR 6m of flight impact, hotels closed two to six months), names the cost of Iran (EUR 40m in Q2, another EUR 20m in Q3), and names the timeline ("I assume until the Middle East and the Far East were back to normal situation" — end of year). That is a manager describing damage, not hiding it.

One further mark of candour, from December 2025 on cruise pricing: "if we would have known that strong demand, we could probably have risen the price by 3%, 4% more." Voluntarily conceding money left on the table is not the behaviour of a promotional management team.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium.** This requires splitting the record in two, because it points in opposite directions.

**The good half — the operating record is strong.**
- August 2025: raised FY25 guidance to 9–11% growth on the back of a record Q3. **Delivered and beat** — FY25 landed at roughly EUR 1.46bn at constant currency, described in December as exceeding the forecast.
- The screener's beat rate of **5 of 7 quarters (71%)** is consistent with this.
- Four straight years of guided-and-delivered profit growth.
- There is a mild **sandbagging pattern** in the good years: the August 2025 raise came alongside an "ad hoc statement yesterday evening," meaning the number was already known to be beating when the range was lifted. That is conservative guiding, which is a virtue, not a vice.

**The bad half — and it is recent and it is material.**

On **10 February 2026** the company reaffirmed FY26 growth of 7–10%. On **22 April 2026** — approximately ten weeks later — it cut to EUR 1.1–1.4bn and **suspended revenue guidance entirely**. At the May call Ebel pre-empted the obvious objection: "You could rightly ask why is the range from EUR 1.1 billion and EUR 1.4 billion, a significant one because the visibility is not as much as we are used to it."

He is right that the honest answer is visibility. But a EUR 300m range on a roughly EUR 1.2bn number is not guidance — it is an admission that the company cannot forecast its own year with four and a half months to run. And the reaffirmation ten weeks earlier means one of two things is true: either February's confidence was not evidence-based, or the Iran war did EUR 300m+ of damage to the forward book between February and April. The transcript supports mostly the second reading (the March disruption is specific and dated — two ships stuck in the Gulf for ten weeks, repatriation flights to the Dubai-Saudi border), but the February reaffirmation was already being made *after* the Jamaica hurricane and *into* a visibly deteriorating Middle East.

**The distinction that matters for sizing:** TUI's guidance misses are **macro-driven, promptly disclosed, and specifically quantified**. They are not the kind that reveals a broken control environment or a management team discovering its own numbers late. But they establish that this management cannot see two quarters ahead in its own business — which is a structural property of a late-booking, geopolitically-exposed tour operator, not a personal failing.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The question management keeps not answering: why is the cruise price not going up?**

Richard Clarke (Bernstein, Feb 2026): "why are prices not growing in the Cruise business?" Asked again in December 2025. Ebel's answer is disarming but is not an answer: "that is a question we put to the management there." A business running 100% occupancy — "in summer last year, 108%. So maybe we even had too many kids on board" — that cannot raise price is either contractually pre-sold or is choosing volume. Management says it is pre-sold ("Fortunately, we are very well sold… the impact is limited"). If that is right, the pricing upside is a 2027–28 event, not a 2026 one. Analysts have pushed on this three calls running and have not got a crisp answer.

**The question analysts keep asking that management resents: Markets & Airline.**

Ebel, February 2026, unusually sharp: "I'm always a little bit puzzled by so many questions comes to Markets + Airlines. The main driver for us is the Holiday Experiences business." The analysts are not confused — they are asking because it is the swing factor. Cristian Nedelcu (UBS) pressed hardest and most usefully in February: given summer booked revenue down 2%, "what gives you confidence that you can indeed grow the EBIT in a strong way year-over-year?" That question **aged into the April guidance cut** — by April, Markets & Airline summer booked revenue was down 7%, not 2%. The analyst was right to push and management's confidence was misplaced.

**The topic that turned into bad news exactly as flagged.** The February 2026 exchange on booking trends and the reliance on a back-ended summer ("this is more back-ended very naturally. So, this is more towards the Summer where we expect then the profit growth" — Kiep, Dec 2025) was the tell. A back-ended year with no visibility is a year that can be taken away by one quarter of geopolitics, and it was.

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing:**
1. **Free cash flow.** Four calls; management discusses earnings, net debt and interest expense fluently, and free cash flow barely at all. Meanwhile it is down 17.4% year on year. Nedelcu had to ask twice about capital expenditure flexibility (May 2026) and got "we will have that discussion internally."
2. **The fleet disadvantage, self-disclosed.** Ebel, May 2026: "we have a significant disadvantage in our fleet. We have now 60 in the summer out of 100, 737 MAX… we don't have the MAX 10 yet. So we don't have a cost competitive product to the A321neo." That is the chief executive stating that a competitor's aircraft is structurally cheaper to fly than most of his own, with "another year to go." No analyst pushed on the size of that gap.
3. **Payment terms.** Nedelcu (May 2026) raised UK competitors loosening payment terms. Ebel's answer was a refusal dressed as a principle: "if you start to manage a company for cash, then it's difficult to get the ghost into the bottle again." Correct in spirit — but a levered tour operator declining a working-capital lever while rivals pull it is a share-loss risk he did not price.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**🔴 Red flags**

- **🔴 The February-to-April guidance collapse (Feb 2026 → 22 Apr 2026).** Reaffirmed 7–10% growth; cut ten weeks later to a range implying anything from −22% to flat, and suspended revenue guidance. The most consequential fact in this file.
- **🔴 Group return on invested capital of 0.4% against segment returns of 17–22% (Dec 2025).** The value created inside the hotels and ships is not arriving at the group level. Something in between — leverage, the airline, minority interests, leases — is eating it.
- **🔴 Free cash flow falling while earnings rise** (−17.4% year on year; −14.1% three-year compound; trailing EUR 722m). The "3.7x free cash flow" cheapness is a multiple on a shrinking denominator.
- **🔴 Altman-Z of 1.4 — distress zone**, with EUR 3.02bn of net debt including EUR 2.32bn of capitalised leases, against a EUR 3.6bn market capitalisation. The debt is larger than the equity.
- **🔴 Return on equity of 99% is a broken-balance-sheet artifact** (EUR −6.47bn accumulated other comprehensive losses). It will mislead any mechanical quality screen.
- **🔴 Insider buy ratio 0.00.** Across a year in which the chief executive repeatedly said "investment in TUI is a great thing" (Dec 2025), no insider bought. Words are cheap; this is the price of them.
- **🔴 Self-disclosed structural fleet cost disadvantage** with "another year to go" (May 2026).
- **🔴 Single-point macro dependence.** Iran, kerosene, and the European consumer. The May call attributes the entire guidance problem to one geopolitical event, and the ceasefire underpinning the recovery expires around mid-August 2026.

**🟢 Green flags**

- **🟢 Four consecutive years of profit growth, delivered** (2022 −EUR 213m loss → 2025 EUR 636m net income). Not a promise — a record.
- **🟢 Real, verifiable deleveraging** (Feb 2026): net debt down EUR 0.5bn year on year, the 2028 convertible repaid **early**, the final Marella ship bought into ownership, total debt down from EUR 6.91bn to EUR 4.47bn in a single quarter. Interest expense improving by roughly EUR 10m as a direct result.
- **🟢 The dividend was restored** and paid (Feb 2026 annual meeting) — the strongest available signal of board confidence in the cash base.
- **🟢 Owned-asset performance is genuinely excellent**: 84% full-year occupancy, 88% in Q4, daily rates up 3–5%, cruise occupancy approaching 100%, 35 million customer database, 70 hotels in the pipeline "mainly management" (fee income, no capital).
- **🟢 Management quantifies its own bad news** (Jamaica EUR 6m, Iran EUR 40m + EUR 20m) and concedes its own errors (cruise pricing left on the table, Dec 2025). This is a credible, non-promotional voice.
- **🟢 The Markets & Airline turnaround is showing first evidence, not just narrative** (Feb 2026: +EUR 10m year on year *including* a −EUR 6m Jamaica hit; May 2026: "the first time for a longer time when we do see a significant improvement"). Belgium and the Netherlands — the chronic problem markets — improved first after the airline commercialisation, which is the specific test the model needed to pass.
- **🟢 The asset-light pivot is real**: 70 hotels in the pipeline are mostly management contracts, which is fee revenue without capital. Ebel pre-empts the resulting optical problem himself — "why is our revenue not growing bigger, because we get the management fee, not the revenue" (Dec 2025).

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The most important terminology shift: "asset-light" became "asset-right."** August 2025 and December 2025 describe hotel growth as an "asset-light model." By May 2026 it is "an asset-right model." That is a small word and a real retreat — it reserves the option to keep putting capital into owned property while retaining the language of discipline. Watch capital expenditure against it.

**Management is describing disintermediation before anyone asks.** Ebel's AI language evolved from a search feature (Aug 2025) to "changing the distribution landscape" and "bringing our own AI agents into LLMs and social media" (May 2026). Read plainly: he expects customers to start their holiday search inside a chatbot rather than on a TUI page, and he intends to be the supplier inside that chatbot rather than the page it replaces. This is the correct response, and it is an implicit admission that the Markets & Airline distribution layer — the 15%-of-profit part — is the structurally threatened one. The owned hotels and ships are not disintermediable in the same way. You can automate a booking form; you cannot automate away a bed in Mallorca that TUI owns.

**"Musement is a wholesale platform now."** The Jet2 partnership (Feb 2026), following Booking.com, easyJet and lastminute.com, is a quiet re-classification: TUI is selling its experiences platform *to its own competitors*. That is a higher-quality, capital-free earnings stream than anything in Markets & Airline, and it is buried in a bullet.

**The new operating structure has a name and a purpose.** May 2026 introduced "a COO function, who makes sure not only to get all the cost and efficiency synergies but also make sure that the sales organization…" — a chief operating officer beneath the chief executive is a normal move, but here it is the enforcement mechanism for the one-airline, one-system consolidation. It also, notably, puts a layer between Ebel and operations for the first time.

**How they talk about competitors changed.** August 2025 used a rival's failure as validation — "you see the example of FTI. As I said, it was a good company, but they were loss-making because they were in a segment where it's really difficult." By May 2026: "It's always difficult to talk about our competitors, and I don't want to do that… I would assume strong brands always benefit from a crisis." The confidence turned generic. Firms stop naming competitors when the comparison stops flattering them.

**A deliberate strategic refusal, stated twice.** TUI will not chase the two- and three-star undifferentiated market — "increased market share would have meant increased losses" (Aug 2025). This caps the growth rate and is almost certainly correct. It also means the company's stated 3%-versus-30% market-share gap in tours and city trips is a genuinely open field: the addressable adjacency is large and unpenetrated.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.**

Not strengthening — the four-year profit-growth streak is being broken this year by the April guidance cut, and free cash flow is falling. Not deteriorating — the transformation is delivering on its own terms, the balance sheet is materially better than a year ago, the dividend is real and paid, and the owned assets are running at record occupancy and rising rates. The operating business is strengthening; the reported earnings trajectory has flattened on macro. Stable is the honest reconciliation.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:**

> **The gap between the quality of the assets and the quality of the claim on them.** TUI's hotels and ships earn 17–22%. TUI's shareholders own a 0.4%-return-on-capital group with EUR 3.02bn of net debt, EUR 1.03bn of minority interests, and an Altman-Z of 1.4 sitting in the distress zone. Every euro of excellence at the property level has to pass through leverage, an unfinished airline rebuild, and other people's stakes before it reaches this share. That is why the stock is cheap, and it is *not* purely a mistake. Size this as a levered claim on a good operating business, not as a cheap good business.

The second-order point: the entire near-term outcome rests on **one shared macro factor** — the Middle East. The guidance cut was Iran. The recovery case is Iran normalising. The ceasefire underpinning it expires around mid-August 2026, which is also roughly when TUI reports its third quarter. A director already carrying oil or geopolitical exposure elsewhere is not adding an independent position here.

**Economic moat: NARROW.**

The moat type is **intangible-brand plus scale-cost through vertical integration**, and it is genuinely present — but it is narrow, not wide.

*The evidence for it being real:* 84% group occupancy rising to 88% in the fourth quarter, "significantly higher than what you see with others" (Dec 2025); daily rates up 3–5% in a soft market; cruise occupancy at or above 100%; a 35-million customer database that makes the marketing cost of filling an owned asset lower than a rival's; a 40% two-year customer retention rate; and a distribution arm that guarantees the assets are full without paying an online travel agency a toll. That last point is the whole model, and it works.

*The evidence for it being narrow, not wide:* group return on invested capital of **0.4%** and gross margin of **9.2%, described as stable**. A wide moat converts pricing power into rising group returns. TUI's occupancy and daily rates rose and its gross margin did not move. The moat is real at the property, and it is being consumed before it reaches the group.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Occupancy up, rates up, margins flat, returns low but not falling; the vertical-integration advantage is being extended (one airline, one system, Musement wholesaling to rivals) rather than eroded. This is not a franchise in decay — but nor is it compounding. The direction of travel is sideways with an option on the cost programme.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.**

The credible structural threat is **artificial-intelligence disintermediation of travel distribution** — the risk that a chatbot books the holiday and the tour operator's storefront becomes redundant. Two facts contain it:

1. It attacks the **wrong 15%**. Distribution (Markets & Airline) is roughly 15% of profit and already the lowest-margin part. Over 80% of profit comes from *owning the product* — hotels, ships, experiences. An AI agent can replace a booking page; it cannot replace a bed TUI owns or a ship TUI operates. If anything, an agent-mediated world raises the value of owning differentiated supply and lowers the value of the shelf — which is the half TUI has been buying and the half it has been shrinking.
2. Management saw it early and is building toward it rather than defending against it (May 2026: agents inside large language models and social media, not a better website).

The threat is real enough to name and not large enough to impair terminal value. The risk that actually kills this equity is **cyclical and financial — a bad summer against 3.0bn of net debt** — not secular.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?**

**A fear-print on a levered asset — which is a third thing, and the director should hold it as such.** The base is not structurally shrinking: revenue is growing, earnings have compounded four years, occupancy and rates are rising, and the debt is falling. That rules out the value trap. But the discount is not a pure mispricing either: a 0.4% return on capital, an Altman-Z of 1.4, falling free cash flow, a self-disclosed fleet cost disadvantage, and zero insider buying are the market pricing a real, correctly-identified fragility. The cheapness is *earned*, roughly two-thirds of it. The remaining third — the part where a market that has watched four years of delivery still refuses to underwrite year five — is the opportunity, and it will not pay out until the summer season is on the tape.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 3 | TRAJECTORY: STABLE | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that TUI is a genuinely good business wearing a bad balance sheet, and the market is still pricing the balance sheet it had in 2021 rather than the one it has now.

Start with what is not in dispute. TUI has grown profits four years running: a EUR 2.48bn loss in 2021, a EUR 213m loss in 2022, then EUR 306m, EUR 507m and EUR 636m of net income through 2025. Revenue reached EUR 24.18bn last year. Trailing-twelve-month earnings per share are EUR 1.26, so at EUR 7.10 the shares change hands for about 5.6 times what the company actually earns today. That is not a forecast; it is the tape.

The engine underneath is the part the market keeps ignoring. Over 80% of profit comes from what TUI calls Holiday Experiences — 463 owned or managed hotels, 18 cruise ships, and the Musement experiences marketplace. Those assets ran at 84% occupancy across the full year and 88% in the fourth quarter (December 2025 call), which management noted is "significantly higher than what you see with others", with daily rates up 3% to 5% in a soft market. Cruise returns were stated at 22% and 17%. Occupancy on the ships is at or above 100% — the chief executive volunteered that last summer hit 108%, "so maybe we even had too many kids on board". The reason these assets stay full is the second half of the model: TUI owns its own shops, apps and airlines, so it fills its own beds without paying an online travel agency a toll. A 35-million-customer database does the marketing that a rival has to buy.

The balance sheet is the part that has actually changed, and it is verifiable rather than narrated. Between December 2025 and March 2026 total debt fell from EUR 6.91bn to EUR 4.47bn. Net debt is down about EUR 0.5bn year on year. The 2028 convertible bond was repaid early. The final Marella cruise ship was bought out of its lease into ownership. Interest expense is improving by roughly EUR 10m a year as a direct consequence. And in February 2026 the company paid its first dividend in years — the single hardest signal a board can send about the durability of its cash, because unlike a forecast it costs real money.

The transformation has also started to show first evidence rather than first slides. Markets & Airline — five or six separate national airlines being welded into one, with one booking system, one buying system and a single web platform — improved by EUR 10m year on year in the first quarter of 2026 even while absorbing a EUR 6m hit from the Jamaica hurricane. Belgium and the Netherlands, the chronic problem markets, turned first after the airline was given commercial control, which is precisely the test the model had to pass. Denied-boarding compensation is running at a third of its former level simply because a Belgian aircraft can now cover a German grounding.

There are three free options the market is not paying for. First, cruise pricing: the business is sold out and cannot raise price this year because the inventory is already booked, but management has conceded it could have charged 3% to 4% more — that is a 2027 and 2028 repricing, not a lost opportunity. Second, the tours and city-trips adjacency, where TUI holds 3% and 5% share of markets it believes should be 30% — an unpenetrated field it is entering with a preproduced round-trip product. Third, Musement is now wholesaling its platform to Booking.com, easyJet, lastminute.com and, since February 2026, Jet2 — capital-free fee income sold to TUI's own competitors, buried in a bullet point.

For this to work, three conditions must hold. The Middle East must normalise so that Eastern Mediterranean and long-haul demand returns — management assumes this takes until the end of the calendar year. Kerosene must stay where it is; Brent at roughly USD 71 is a live tailwind against the fuel costs that caused the April downgrade in the first place. And the cost programme must convert on schedule, with the single web platform reaching Germany in January or February 2027.

If all three hold, this is a company earning EUR 1.5bn or more before interest and tax on a EUR 3.6bn market value, still deleveraging, still paying a dividend, and priced at roughly five times earnings.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require TUI to be a bad company. It requires only that the shareholder's claim on a good company is thinner than it looks — and that the balance sheet does not permit a second bad year.

Start with the number that indicts everything else. Management quotes cruise returns of 22% and 17%. The group's return on invested capital is 0.4%. Both are true, and the gap between them is the entire bear case. The excellence exists at the property; it does not arrive at the group. What stands in between is EUR 3.02bn of net debt (including EUR 2.32bn of capitalised leases), EUR 1.03bn of minority interests in businesses like the Riu hotel joint venture, and an airline still halfway through being rebuilt. Every euro of hotel margin passes through all of that before it reaches this share. That is why the discount exists, and it is largely correct.

The cheapness is measured against numbers that are going the wrong way. The stock screens at 3.7 times free cash flow — but free cash flow fell 17.4% year on year and is compounding at negative 14.1% over three years, from roughly EUR 991m in 2025 to EUR 722m trailing. Earnings per share are rising while cash generation falls. A low multiple on a shrinking denominator is not a bargain, it is arithmetic. Across four earnings calls, management discussed profit, net debt and interest expense fluently and free cash flow almost not at all; when a UBS analyst pushed twice on capital-expenditure flexibility in May 2026, the answer was "we will have that discussion internally".

The headline quality metric is fake. Return on equity of 99% looks like a franchise. It is an artifact of a bombed-out equity base: EUR 7.98bn of paid-in capital sitting against EUR 6.47bn of accumulated other comprehensive losses, leaving EUR 2.02bn of book equity. A 99% return on equity next to a 0.4% return on capital is not a moat; it is a broken denominator. Any mechanical screen ranking this name on returns is being fooled.

The guidance record broke, and recently. On 10 February 2026 TUI reaffirmed 7% to 10% profit growth for the year. On 22 April 2026 — ten weeks later — it cut to a range of EUR 1.1bn to EUR 1.4bn and suspended revenue guidance entirely. Against the 2025 base of about EUR 1.41bn, that range spans a 22% decline to roughly flat. The four-year growth streak, the thing the bull case rests on, is being broken this year. A EUR 300m range with four and a half months of the year remaining is not guidance; it is an admission that the company cannot forecast its own book. The chief executive conceded exactly that: "the visibility is not as much as we are used to it".

And the damage is worse than the headline. Summer 2026 booked revenue in Markets & Airline was down 7% year on year at the April cut, having been down only 2% in August 2025 — the deterioration accelerated. Hotel occupancy for the second half was tracking 7% below the prior year, concentrated in Turkey, Cyprus and Egypt. This is a late-booking business, so the season cannot be pre-sold out of trouble; management flagged that customers "book very late" and that May was merely flat against last year.

The solvency position leaves no room for a second shock. The Altman-Z score of 1.4 sits in the distress zone. Net debt of EUR 3.02bn exceeds a market capitalisation of EUR 3.6bn — the lenders own more of this enterprise than the shareholders do. Deferred revenue of EUR 5.25bn is customer money for holidays not yet taken; in a demand shock that is a refund liability, not a cushion. And there is no rescue coming from rates: the Federal Reserve is on a hawkish hold with markets pricing roughly a 77% chance of a hike by December, which means a levered European cyclical refinances into a worse market, not a better one.

Management has disclosed a structural cost disadvantage it cannot fix quickly. In May 2026: "we have a significant disadvantage in our fleet. We have now 60 in the summer out of 100, 737 MAX… we don't have the MAX 10 yet. So we don't have a cost competitive product to the A321neo", with "another year to go". A tour operator whose aircraft cost more to fly than a rival's, in a business with a 9.2% gross margin, is losing a race it has not finished entering. Separately, Ebel refused to match UK rivals loosening payment terms — principled, and a share-loss risk he did not price.

The pricing power the bulls cite is not showing up where it counts. Occupancy rose. Daily rates rose 3% to 5%. Gross margin was 9.2% and described as stable. The margin did not move. Whatever the hotels are earning is being consumed before it reaches the group line.

Finally, nobody inside is buying. The insider buy ratio is zero across a year in which the chief executive said "investment in TUI is a great thing". The smart-money score is 12 out of 100.

What would confirm the bear: a third-quarter print in August 2026 landing at the bottom of the EUR 1.1bn to EUR 1.4bn range; the mid-August ceasefire expiry re-escalating and taking kerosene with it; or free cash flow turning negative and stalling the deleveraging that is the only thing genuinely working.
consensus_delta:
For a deep-value name the question is not whether the market is excited — it is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company whose earning power is actually stable or growing. Here the honest answer is: partly, and less than it first appears.

**Where the market is genuinely wrong.** The street is still underwriting TUI as the 2021 balance sheet — a company that lost EUR 2.48bn and diluted its owners to survive. That company no longer exists. Total debt fell from EUR 6.91bn to EUR 4.47bn in the single quarter to March 2026. The 2028 convertible bond was repaid *early* — a levered borrower with a liquidity problem does not retire debt ahead of schedule. The final Marella ship was bought out of its lease into ownership. A dividend was paid in February 2026. Four consecutive years of profit growth were delivered, not promised. That is a company actively repairing itself, and it trades at 5.6 times what it earns.

**Where the market is right and this committee will not pretend otherwise.** The peer check kills the easy version of the trade. Jet2, the closest listed comparable, trades at 7.18 times earnings today with *net cash*. TUI trades at 5.6 times with EUR 3.02bn of net debt. The discount is roughly 21% and it is exactly what leverage should cost. There is no 80% mispricing here — the screener's +81% discounted-cash-flow margin of safety is an artifact of extrapolating cash flow that is in fact *falling* 17.4% a year. The whole European package-holiday lane has de-rated together on the same drivers. Cheap versus its own history is not the same as cheap versus the world.

**The specific street assumption that is wrong.** Published targets cluster around EUR 10.2 to 10.4, with Morgan Stanley at EUR 10.50 (trimmed from EUR 11.50) and Jefferies stepping back to neutral after the recent rally. Those numbers embed a recovery to the guided growth path. But nobody appears to have re-anchored to what the peer group actually trades at *now*: at Jet2's live 7.18 times, TUI's trailing earnings support EUR 9.05, and a sum-of-the-parts built from management's own 80/15 profit split, charged properly for EUR 3.02bn of net debt and EUR 1.03bn of minority interests, independently gives EUR 9.06. Two methods, one cent apart. The street is roughly 12% too high, not too low — the market is closer to right than the analysts are.

**The real disagreement, and it is narrow.** The market is treating a 0.4% return on invested capital as the company's earning power. It is not — it is the *shareholder's claim* on a business whose hotels and ships earn 17% to 22%. The distinction matters, and the market conflates the two. But the conflation is only about two-thirds wrong. A director owning this share genuinely does receive the leftovers after EUR 3.02bn of debt, EUR 1.03bn of minorities and an unfinished airline take their cut. The gap between EUR 7.10 and EUR 9.10 is what the market is missing. It is real, it is about 28%, and it is not the multi-bagger the screener advertises.
forcing_function:
**The near-dated event: third-quarter results, on or about 12 August 2026** (roughly 27 days from the scan date). This is the only dated event on the board and it is genuinely forcing — not because it is contractual, but because it is arithmetically cornered. The company must narrow a EUR 1.1bn to EUR 1.4bn range with only weeks of its financial year remaining, and the third quarter *is* the summer that decides the number. There is nowhere left to hide a EUR 300m spread. Either the range collapses upward, in which case four years of delivery becomes five and the peer discount is exposed as too wide, or it collapses downward and the dividend restored six months ago comes into question.

**Why this is a soft, non-binding catalyst rather than a hard one — and the distinction is doing real work.** The date is real; the *payout* is not fixed by anything. This is a scheduled earnings report whose outcome is decided by a third party — the Middle East — and by kerosene. Nothing contractual pays the shareholder on that date. It is a single macro binary wearing a calendar, and this committee will not dress it up as an asymmetric special situation. Note also that the ceasefire clock expires around the same mid-August window: the resolution driver and the reporting date are the same factor arriving twice, which concentrates risk rather than diversifying it.

**The catalyst that has already fired, and must not be counted twice.** The dividend initiation — announced December 2025, paid at the February 2026 annual meeting — was the genuine re-rating event for this story. It is spent. Any thesis still leaning on "TUI will restore the dividend" is underwriting a fact from six months ago.

**The slower, more structural forcing functions, in the order they arrive:**
1. **December 2026 — full-year results plus the cost-programme detail.** Management has twice deferred the quantified savings to a December unveiling. The single web platform reaches Germany, the last market, in "January, February '27". December is where 2027 gets guided and where the transformation either prices or does not.
2. **The deleveraging arithmetic itself, continuously.** This is the most reliable engine on the page and it needs no announcement. Net debt down about EUR 0.5bn year on year, the 2028 convertible retired early, ships bought out of leases. With EUR 3.02bn of net debt against a EUR 3.6bn market value, every euro that moves from the lenders' column to the owners' column is worth roughly a euro of equity — mechanically, without any re-rating at all. In a market regime that rewards balance-sheet repair over rate relief, this is the part of the thesis that does not depend on anyone's opinion.
3. **2027–28 cruise pricing.** Sold-out ships that management concedes were underpriced by 3% to 4% reprice as inventory rolls. Real, but two years out and not a catalyst anyone trades.

**What is absent, and should be named.** There is no activist, no strategic review, no announced asset sale, no governance reset, no tender, no sum-of-the-parts breakup process. On the Loeb catalyst-density test this scores poorly: one dated macro-dependent print, one spent dividend, and a slow deleveraging grind. The regime read favours structural special situations in thin lanes — and a levered cyclical waiting on the weather is not one.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are, quite precisely, the risk. This is not a name where you wait through a quiet stretch for a catalyst — the risky window and the catalyst are the same event.

**The season is the whole year, and it is unhedged.** TUI guided its 2026 profit to be "more back-ended very naturally… towards the Summer" (December 2025). That means essentially all of the year's profit is earned between June and September 2026 — the months directly ahead. There is no second attempt. A tour operator cannot re-run a summer.

**And this is a late-booking market, so it cannot be pre-sold out of trouble.** Management flagged that customers now "book very late" and that May was merely level with last year (May 2026). At the April downgrade, Markets & Airline booked revenue for Summer 2026 was 7% below the prior year — having been down only 2% in August 2025. The deterioration is accelerating, and the inventory is risk capacity that must be filled or flown empty.

**The mid-August collision.** Three things land on top of each other. The United States–Iran 60-day ceasefire clock expires around **mid-August 2026** — and it is more fragile than the headline suggests, with a US airstrike on 26 June following an alleged violation and Geneva talks postponed. TUI's **third-quarter results land at roughly the same moment** (about 27 days out from the scan, so approximately 12 August), and that print must narrow a EUR 1.1bn-to-EUR 1.4bn range with only weeks of the year left. Both bear on the same driver. If the ceasefire fails, kerosene rises, the Eastern Mediterranean and long-haul bookings that management already describes as "almost 0" stay at zero, and the print goes to the bottom of the range — all at once, in the same fortnight.

**The cash-flow hump nobody is discussing.** Free cash flow is already falling 17.4% year on year, from roughly EUR 991m to EUR 722m trailing, and management barely mentions it across four calls. Capital expenditure is committed and hard to stop: hotel projects "online and they will be kind of executed", the Boeing delivery portfolio with attached engine and maintenance spend, and two new Marella ships under a signed shipyard contract. When a UBS analyst asked directly in May 2026 how much of that could be cut, the answer was "we will have that discussion internally". That is a company with fixed outflows and a variable summer.

**Deferred revenue is a liability, not a cushion.** There is EUR 5.25bn of customer money on the balance sheet for holidays not yet taken. In a normal season that is free financing. In a demand shock — a re-escalation that makes people cancel rather than book — it converts into a refund obligation at exactly the moment the cash is needed. This is the mechanism that nearly killed the company in 2020, and it is unchanged.

**No rescue from rates.** The Federal Reserve under Chair Warsh is on a hawkish hold with futures pricing roughly a 77% chance of a *hike* by December, and Goldman no longer expects a 2026 cut. A levered European cyclical with EUR 3.02bn of net debt and an Altman-Z of 1.4 refinances into a worse market, not a better one. Any version of this thesis that quietly relies on cheaper money is dead on arrival.

**The one genuine offset.** Brent at roughly USD 71 and West Texas at USD 68.6 are *below* the level that caused the April downgrade — the cut explicitly cited airline fuel costs. Oil deflating is a real, live tailwind into the very season in question, and it is the single best reason the August print could surprise upward rather than downward.
positioning_washout:
